ArmFeedback.description:
Both arms' narrowed feedback from ONE controller feedback frame.

The arm controller reports both sides in a single datagram at its native
rate (1 kHz on hardware, 100 Hz against the simulator), so this is the
unit an observer receives: one frame, two sides. It exists as a core type
so a consumer that only wants to WATCH the arm — the telemetry sampler —
can do so through the core abstraction without depending on the backend
crate's wider `ArmSnapshot`, which additionally carries wire-level fields
(impedance type, commanded pose, configuration-parameter serials) that
only the backend's own command sequencing needs.

a.description: Arm A, the robot's physical LEFT arm.

b.description: Arm B, the robot's physical RIGHT arm.

oneOf.description: The arm is idle.
The arm is in joint-position mode.
The arm is in PVT mode.
The arm is in torque mode.
The arm is released/floating.
The arm controller reports an error.
A controller mode not known by this core version.

unknown.description: A controller mode not known by this core version.

ArmModeRequest.description:
A requested arm control mode.

The two torque-based variants both put the controller into its `TORQ`
state and differ only in the impedance type they select and in the
parameters they send: `CartesianImpedance` selects impedance type 2 and
configures Cartesian stiffness, damping, and end-effector rotation;
`ForceCompliance` selects impedance type 3 and configures a force
direction set, a force loop, and a target contact force.

oneOf.description: Disable position control.
Enter position control with velocity and acceleration ratios.

acc_ratio.description: Acceleration ratio, as a backend-defined normalized ratio.

vel_ratio.description: Velocity ratio, as a backend-defined normalized ratio.

oneOf.description:
Joint impedance in the controller's TORQ state (ImpType=1).
Joint targets remain commandable. Gains are explicit so a caller
supplies the mounted robot's chosen joint stiffness and damping.

acc_ratio.description: Normalized acceleration ratio restored after anchored entry.

damping.description: Joint damping in N m/(degree/s), seven joints.

stiffness.description: Joint stiffness in N m/degree, seven joints.

vel_ratio.description: Normalized velocity ratio restored after anchored entry.

oneOf.description:
Enter Cartesian impedance control: the controller holds the commanded
pose through a spring-damper acting in Cartesian space, so the end
effector yields to external force and returns.

Every field defaults to the reference implementation's own value; an
omitted field is therefore a request for that default rather than for
zero.

acc_ratio.description:
Acceleration ratio restored once the mode is live, as a normalized
ratio.

eef_rotation.description: End-effector rotation parameters forwarded to the controller.

stiffness.description:
Cartesian stiffness. Indices `0..=5` are the X, Y, Z, Rx, Ry, Rz
stiffnesses; index `6` is the null-space stiffness for the arm's
redundant seventh joint, not a seventh Cartesian axis.

vel_ratio.description:
Velocity ratio restored once the mode is live, as a normalized
ratio. Mode entry itself always runs at a fixed reduced ratio.

oneOf.description:
Enter force/compliance control: the controller yields along the
enabled Cartesian directions, optionally pressing with a target force.

Every field defaults to the reference implementation's own value.

acc_ratio.description:
Acceleration ratio restored once the mode is live, as a normalized
ratio.

adjustment_limit_mm.description:
How far, in millimetres, the controller may displace the end
effector in order to comply. This is the softness knob: a larger
value makes the arm more backdrivable. Must be positive.

anchor_command_pose.description:
Write the measured pose into the controller's commanded pose
immediately before the transition. On by default, and unsafe to
turn off: the commanded pose persists in the controller, so
without anchoring, engaging torque tells the arm to drive to
whatever pose was left there.

control_params.description:
Force-loop gains and limits. All zeros selects the controller's
built-in defaults, which is the supported configuration.

force_direction.description:
Which Cartesian directions (X, Y, Z, Rx, Ry, Rz) the force loop
acts on; `1` enables a direction and `0` disables it. At least one
direction must be enabled.

force_type.description:
Force-control strategy selector; the reference implementation uses
zero.

target_force.description:
Target contact force in newtons, and the field to leave at zero
unless the end effector is against something that can react.

This is an active command, not a sensitivity threshold: any
positive value makes the controller push along `force_direction`
until it measures that force, which in free space never happens,
so the arm creeps continuously. Zero means pure compliance — hold
the pose, yield to contact. Must not be negative.

vel_ratio.description:
Velocity ratio restored once the mode is live, as a normalized
ratio.

zero_wrist_roll.description:
Command the wrist-roll joint (J7) to zero as part of the entry
anchor, rather than freezing it at whatever angle the arm arrived
in.

The joint is equally stiff either way — the default direction set
enables no rotation — but this changes the angle it is stiff at.
It commands a motion at entry, so it is off by default.

ChassisState.description:
Chassis feedback, including whether the mobile base is there at all.

A D1 is regularly run with its vendor chassis powered off — on external
power, using only the lift, arms, torso and head. The chassis controller is
then a dead HTTP origin, and every request to it costs a full connect
timeout. [`ChassisState::available`] is the daemon's standing answer to
"is the base there", decided by a bounded startup probe and re-checked on a
timer, so a caller can skip its chassis steps outright rather than
discovering the absence one timeout at a time.

availability_reason.description:
Why [`ChassisState::available`] holds its current value: the transport
error for an absent base, the configuration for one declared absent,
and a short confirmation for a reachable one.

available.description:
Whether the chassis controller answered the last availability check.

`false` means every chassis command and query is refused immediately
with `unavailable` and NOTHING is sent to the network; the rest of this
structure is then the default reading, not a measurement. Consumers
that orchestrate the robot should read this field and skip their
chassis steps rather than issuing commands that cannot succeed.

emergency_stop.description: Whether the chassis emergency stop is active.

last_probe_unix_ms.description:
Milliseconds since the UNIX epoch at which the last availability check
settled, or `0` when none has run (a backend that does not probe).

omega.description: Angular velocity in radians per second; positive is counter-clockwise.

vx.description: Forward velocity in metres per second; negative is reverse.

changed.description: Whether any joint differs exactly from its supplied value.

clamped_deg.description: The seven clamped joint angles in degrees, or an empty vector for an invalid request.

One controller fault scanned from the vendor `LOG.txt` tail.

The originating log line is kept verbatim in `raw` because a fault log is

EyeCommand.description:
One eye command: which strips to address, plus the effect to run on them.

This is the wire shape of `POST /v1/eyes/cmd` and of the `eyes.cmd`
WebSocket method: `target` and the internally tagged [`EyeEffect`] share
one flat object, for example
`{"target": "left", "effect": "solid", "r": 0, "g": 0, "b": 255}`.

EyeEffect.description:
An eye LED effect.

The enum is internally tagged by `effect`, matching the command vocabulary
used by the REST and WebSocket frontends.  Effect-layer validation of the
`step` range belongs to the eye backend; the core preserves the requested
byte values.

oneOf.description: A breathing effect with an RGB color, step size, and delay.
A running-light effect with an RGB color, window length, and delay.
A solid RGB color.
Clear the selected strip.
Stop the selected strip's active effect.

EyeTarget.description: Selects which eye LED strip receives an effect.

percent.description:
Battery percentage `0..=100`, clamped into that range.  `null` clears
the gauge.  Non-finite values may also be sent as the strings `nan`,
`inf` or `-inf`, which JSON itself cannot represent.

loops.description:
Loop count; omitted means `0`, which defers to the document's own
loop policy.  The service ceiling is 20 loops.

name.description: Catalog expression name, as listed by `GET /v1/eyes/list_expressions`.

EyesPixelRequest.description:
One frozen-window single-pixel placement request.

`index` is the LED index as the eye controller counts the strip
(`0..=17`), `target` names one eye (`left` or `right`; `both` is refused
because the two strips do not run a `BOTH`-addressed window in phase), and
`delay_ms` is the window speed in milliseconds per index, defaulting to
the measured 100 ms.

delay_ms.description:
Window speed in milliseconds per index; omitted selects the measured
100 ms default.

target.description: Which eye strip to place the pixel on; `both` is refused.

GripPreset.description:
Named grip-force presets for a gripper stroke.

The backend maps each to a standing hold preload in motor radians; `firm`
is the configured default, `strong` the largest preload the mechanism is
allowed to hold with.

GripRequest.description:
How hard a closing stroke holds what it meets.

At most one of the two fields is given: a named [`GripPreset`], or an
explicit standing preload in motor radians. Neither means the backend's
configured default. Carried by [`GripperTarget`] and by a bare `close`.

oneOf.description: A named preset.

grip_preload_rad.description: An explicit standing preload, in motor radians.

coil_c.description: Coil temperature in °C from a live reading, when one was taken.

grip_preload_rad.description:
Standing preload the hold keeps, in motor radians; zero when nothing
is held.

holding.description: Whether the report indicates an object is held.

jaw_rad.description: Measured jaw position in motor radians.

live.description:
Whether `jaw_rad` and `torque_nm` are a live reading of the idle motor
(true) or the last stroke's telemetry (false, motor busy or silent).

open_rad.description: Configured open ceiling in motor radians, when published by the backend.

GripperSlot.description:
Either the device's own state or, when that device could not be
read, a [`SlotError`] naming the failure.

oneOf.description: The device answered; this is its state.
The device could not be read.

GripperSlots.description: The two grippers' slots, keyed by side.

allOf.description: How hard to hold an object met on the way.

closedness.description: Fraction of the stroke from open (0) to closed (1).

jaw_rad.description: Absolute jaw position in motor radians.

GripperTarget.description:
A continuous gripper target.

Exactly one of `closedness` and `jaw_rad` is given. `closedness` is the hand-protocol
convention shared with dx-manipulator's wire units: `0.0` is the commanded
open ceiling, `1.0` the closed stop, linear in motor radians between them.
`jaw_rad` addresses the motor directly, in the same radians the stroke
report's `jaw_rad` uses. The backend resolves either to a motor target and
refuses values outside the mechanism's range. The flattened
[`GripRequest`] fields (`grip`, `grip_preload_rad`) say how hard to hold
whatever the stroke meets on the way.

The wire spelling is the `"<maker>/<model>"` id the retiring

The most recent device error record: `0` means none. On the O30 this

Capability tokens, repeated here so a consumer that only polls state

Whether `positions` came from a reading taken for THIS call, rather
than from the last one the command path happened to take.

A read on these hands is not free — it competes with the command path
for the arm's single passthrough channel — so a busy hand answers
with its last sample and says so here, exactly as the gripper's
report does.

kill.description:
Every device's soft-kill latch.  This slot never degrades: it is
daemon-local state, not a device read.

SoftKillAction.description: One stop action issued by a soft kill, and what became of it.

action.description:
Dotted action name, such as `arm.a.emergency_stop` or

detail.description: Why, when the outcome is not `ok`. Absent on success.

elapsed_ms.description:
Milliseconds from the moment the kill was raised to this action
settling.

Every action is issued concurrently, so these are elapsed times from
one shared origin rather than a sum: an arm that stopped in 3 ms next
to a chassis that timed out at 1000 ms is the join working as
intended, not 1003 ms of kill latency.

SoftKillOutcome.description: What one soft-kill stop action did.

SoftKillReport.description:
The outcome of one whole soft kill.

The latch — the part that is always effective, applied before any stop is
issued — is in `latched`; `actions` is what each device's stop-shaped verb
then did. A kill whose report contains failures is still a kill: nothing
new is admitted for any device in `latched`.

actions.description: Every stop action, in a stable order.

latched.description: The latch map as it stands after the kill; every device is latched.

Responses can arrive out of order (see [`WsResponse`]), so this is the
only way to match a response to its request.

method.description:
The `x-ws-method` value of the operation to call, for example
`arm.a.move_joints`.  Side-templated operations are spelled with a
concrete side: `arm.a.mode`, never `arm.{side}.mode`.

params.description: The operation's request body, as an object.  Omitted means `{}`.

WsResponse.description:
One response frame, carrying the same payload the REST envelope would.

**Responses are not ordered.**  Each request is dispatched on its own
task, so a long motion call never delays another request on the same
connection and a later request can answer first.  Correlate by `id`, never
by arrival order.

data.description:
The operation's result on success, null on error.  This is the same
payload as the REST envelope's `data` for the same method.

id.description:
The `id` of the request this answers, or null when the frame could not
be parsed far enough to recover one.

message.description: The failure reason on error, null on success.

WsSoftKillEvent.description:
An unsolicited frame pushed when one device's soft-kill latch changes.

It has no `id`: it answers no request.  Distinguish pushes from responses
by the presence of `event`.

killed.description: The device's latch value after the transition.

info.description:
The `d1-firmwared` HTTP API: one guarded surface over the D1's arms, grippers, pan/tilt neck, eye LED controller, vertical slider and mobile chassis.

## This API is unauthenticated

The daemon performs **no authentication and no authorization of any kind**. Every caller that can open the port can move a 110 kg robot. It binds the loopback interface by default; keep it there. To reach it from another host, tunnel it over SSH or an equivalently authenticated channel — do not bind it to a routable address and do not put it behind a bare reverse proxy. The `security: []` below is a statement of fact, not an omission.

## Ratios are fractions, not percentages

Every `vel_ratio` and `acc_ratio` field is a **fraction of full speed in `0.0..=1.0`**. `0.1` means 10% of full speed. `100` does not mean 100%: it is out of range and is rejected with a 400. This has caused a real full-speed-arm incident on a robot, which is why the value is now refused rather than clamped.

## Every response is enveloped

Except `GET /v1/chassis/map_image`, which returns raw `image/png` on success, every response body is `{"status", "data", "message"}`. `status` is `ok` or `error`; `message` is always present and is `null` on success; `data` is `null` for commands that return nothing, and `null` on every error. Unknown routes and unknown methods answer with the same 404 envelope rather than a framework 404 or 405.

## Blocking calls

Several operations block for real robot motion. Each carries an `x-timeout-seconds` extension giving the longest it is expected to take, so a generated client can size its own timeout: the slider's `set_height` with `wait: true` can take five minutes, gripper strokes about 40 seconds, arm recovery about 65 seconds, and a waited joint move about 30 seconds. A client default of a few seconds will time out on a call that is working correctly.

## The same verbs over WebSocket

The WebSocket frontend (default `ws://127.0.0.1:4751/ws`) speaks the same verbs over one persistent connection. An operation callable that way carries an `x-ws-method` extension naming the method to put in a `WsRequest`; an operation without one is REST-only. Requests are dispatched concurrently, so **responses can arrive out of order** — correlate them by `id`, never by arrival order. The connection also pushes unsolicited `WsSoftKillEvent` and `WsNavEvent` frames, told apart from responses by their `event` field.

## Clients are generated, not shipped

This document is the deliverable. See the repository README for the exact commands for `openapi-python-client`, `openapi-typescript` + `openapi-fetch`, and `progenitor`.

post.description: The COMPLETE emergency stop of everything this daemon owns, in one call: both arms, both grippers, both hands, the neck, the eyes, the slider and the chassis (zero velocity, navigation paused, light strip off). Do not implement a device-by-device kill above this route. Every latch is set before any stop is issued and the stops run concurrently, so one wedged device cannot delay another; the response reports each action as `ok`, `failed`, `timeout` or `unavailable`, with the milliseconds it took. The chassis actions are bounded at 1 s each and are skipped without any network I/O when the base is known to be absent, so this call returns promptly even against a wedged or missing base. The latch is sticky: motion verbs are refused with 409 until `/v1/release_soft_kill`. This is not a substitute for the physical emergency stop.

get.description: Reads all six devices concurrently. The call never fails as a whole: a device that cannot be read degrades to `{"error": "..."}` in its own slot while the rest of the snapshot is still returned, so check each slot rather than only the HTTP status.
